sections.title: Introduction to Electrostatics
sections.narration: Welcome to the world of electrostatics! At its very core, electricity is all about a fundamental property of matter called charge. You've seen its effects everywhere - from a spark when you touch a doorknob on a dry day, to a lightning strike in a storm. The classical study of electricity is typically divided into three main areas. First, we have Electrostatics, which is the focus of this chapter. This is the study of stationary charges and the forces that act between them. Imagine charges that are fixed in place, not moving. We'll explore the fields and potentials they create. Next is Electric Current, which you might be more familiar with. This is the study of charges in motion, flowing through circuits to power our devices, from light bulbs to smartphones. It’s all about the energy associated with the flow of charge. Finally, there's Electromagnetism, which explores the fascinating link between electricity and magnetism, studying the forces that arise when charges are in motion. Together, these three areas form the foundation of our understanding of electricity. In this lesson, we will dive deep into the first of these: electrostatics, the science of static charges.

sections.title: The Concept of Charge
sections.narration: So what exactly is this 'charge' we keep talking about? It comes in two, and only two, types: positive and negative. These names, by the way, were arbitrarily assigned by Benjamin Franklin. We denote them with a plus sign for positive and a minus sign for negative. Now, it's crucial to understand that the term 'neutral' doesn't mean a third type of charge. A neutral object is simply one that has an equal amount of positive and negative charge, so their effects cancel each other out. To understand where charge comes from, we need to look at the atomic level. In nature, atoms are normally electrically neutral. They have a nucleus with positively charged protons, and an equal number of negatively charged electrons orbiting that nucleus. The charge on a single proton and a single electron are equal in magnitude but opposite in sign. In fact, the charge on an electron is the smallest amount of free charge ever discovered. We build up a net charge on an object by either adding or removing these electrons. If we remove electrons from a neutral object, it's left with more protons than electrons, resulting in a net positive charge. Conversely, if we add extra electrons to a neutral object, it will have an excess of electrons, resulting in a net negative charge. So, remember: a positively charged body has lost electrons, and a negatively charged body has gained electrons.

sections.title: Basic Properties of Charge
sections.narration: Electric charge has several fundamental properties that govern its behavior. First, charge is a scalar quantity, meaning it has magnitude but no direction. And since there are two types, positive and negative, they add up algebraically. If you have a system with +5 units of charge and you add -2 units, the net charge is simply +3 units. Second, and this is a cornerstone of physics, charge is conserved. In any isolated system, the net electric charge remains constant. This means charge cannot be created or destroyed, only transferred from one object to another. We see this principle in action in many physical processes. For example, in the radioactive decay of a Uranium-238 nucleus, it splits into Thorium-234 and a Helium nucleus. The initial charge of 92 elementary units is perfectly conserved, as Thorium has 90 and Helium has 2. In an annihilation process, an electron (charge -e) and its antiparticle, a positron (charge +e), collide. Their total initial charge is zero. They annihilate and produce high-energy photons, which have no charge, so the total final charge is also zero. The reverse is also true. In pair production, a high-energy photon with zero charge can convert into an electron and a positron pair near a nucleus. Again, the net charge before and after the event is zero. This conservation law is absolute and has never been observed to be violated.

segments.text: Electric charge has several fundamental properties that govern its behavior. First, charge is a scalar quantity, meaning it has magnitude but no direction. And since there are two types, positive and negative, they add up algebraically.
If you have a system with +5 units of charge and you add -2 units, the net charge is simply +3 units.

Second, and this is a cornerstone of physics, charge is conserved. In any isolated system, the net electric charge remains constant. This means charge cannot be created or destroyed, only transferred from one object to another.
We see this principle in action in many physical processes. For example, in the radioactive decay of a Uranium-238 nucleus, it splits into Thorium-234 and a Helium nucleus.
The initial charge of 92 elementary units is perfectly conserved, as Thorium has 90 and Helium has 2.
In an annihilation process, an electron (charge -e) and its antiparticle, a positron (charge +e), collide. Their total initial charge is zero.
They annihilate and produce high-energy photons, which have no charge, so the total final charge is also zero.

The reverse is also true. In pair production, a high-energy photon with zero charge can convert into an electron and a positron pair near a nucleus. Again, the net charge before and after the event is zero.
This conservation law is absolute and has never been observed to be violated.

sections.title: Quantization of Charge
sections.narration: The third fundamental property of charge is that it is quantized. This groundbreaking discovery was made by Robert Millikan through his famous oil drop experiment. Quantization means that electric charge doesn't come in any arbitrary amount; it exists in discrete packets. The smallest packet of free charge is the charge of a single electron, which we denote by the symbol 'e'. Any observable charge on an object, which we call 'q', must be an integer multiple of this fundamental unit. This relationship is expressed by the simple formula q equals N times e, where N is an integer—it can be 1, 2, 3, and so on, but it cannot be a fraction. This means the charge on a body can be 1e, 2e, -5e, or 1 million e, but it can never be something like one-third of 'e' or 2.5 times 'e'. This is because charge is transferred by moving whole electrons; you can't move half an electron. Now, you might have heard about quarks, which are fundamental particles that make up protons and neutrons. Quarks do have fractional charges, like plus or minus e/3 or 2e/3. However, quarks are never found in isolation in nature; they are always bound together inside larger particles. Therefore, for all practical purposes and for any free charge we can measure, the principle of quantization holds true with the fundamental unit being the charge of an electron, 'e'.

sections.title: More Properties of Charge
sections.narration: Let's cover a few more essential properties of charge. A very famous one is that similar charges repel each other, while opposite charges attract. So, two positive charges will push each other away, as will two negative charges. But a positive and a negative charge will pull towards each other. It’s important to note that the true test of whether an object is charged, or 'electrified', is repulsion. Why? Because attraction can also occur between a charged body and a neutral one through a process called induction, which we'll discuss soon. Repulsion, however, only happens between two objects with like charges. Another key point is that charge is always associated with mass. A particle must have mass to carry a charge. The reverse isn't true; a particle can have mass but be neutral, like a neutron. Also, charge is transferable. It can move from one object to another upon contact, a process called conduction. Furthermore, charge is invariant. This means an object's charge doesn't change no matter how fast it's moving. A charge of 1 coulomb at rest is still 1 coulomb when moving near the speed of light. This is different from mass, which increases with velocity according to relativity. The effects produced by a charge depend on its state of motion. A charge at rest produces only an electric field. A charge in uniform, unaccelerated motion produces both an electric and a magnetic field. And an accelerated charge does both, plus it radiates energy in the form of electromagnetic waves. Finally, for a conductor, any excess charge will reside on its outer surface. There is no net charge inside the material of a conductor in electrostatic equilibrium.

sections.title: Units of Charge
sections.narration: Now that we know what charge is, how do we measure it? The standard international, or SI, unit for measuring electric charge is the coulomb, abbreviated with a capital C. But what is one coulomb? It's actually a derived unit, defined based on electric current. You may recall that electric current is the rate of flow of charge. Mathematically, current 'I' is charge 'q' divided by time 't'. We can rearrange this to define charge: q equals I times t. From this, we can define one coulomb: it is the amount of charge that flows past a point in a conductor in one second when the current is one ampere. So, one coulomb is equal to one ampere-second. To give you some perspective, the fundamental charge 'e'—the charge of a single proton or electron—is incredibly small. The charge on a proton is positive 1.6 times 10 to the power of minus 19 coulombs, and an electron's charge is the negative of that. This means you would need a staggering 6.25 quintillion electrons—that's 6.25 times 10 to the power of 18—to make up a total charge of just negative one coulomb. While the coulomb is the SI unit, you might encounter other units. In the CGS system, there's the 'esu' or electrostatic unit, also called the statcoulomb. One coulomb is equal to 3 times 10 to the power of 9 esu. For practical applications, especially with batteries, you might see units like the Ampere-hour, which is 3600 coulombs, or the Faraday, used in chemistry, which is about 96,500 coulombs.

segments.text: Now that we know what charge is, how do we measure it? The standard international, or SI, unit for measuring electric charge is the coulomb, abbreviated with a capital C.
But what is one coulomb? It's actually a derived unit, defined based on electric current. You may recall that electric current is the rate of flow of charge.
Mathematically, current 'I' is charge 'q' divided by time 't'. We can rearrange this to define charge: q equals I times t.
From this, we can define one coulomb: it is the amount of charge that flows past a point in a conductor in one second when the current is one ampere. So, one coulomb is equal to one ampere-second.

To give you some perspective, the fundamental charge 'e'—the charge of a single proton or electron—is incredibly small. The charge on a proton is positive 1.6 times 10 to the power of minus 19 coulombs, and an electron's charge is the negative of that.
This means you would need a staggering 6.25 quintillion electrons—that's 6.25 times 10 to the power of 18—to make up a total charge of just negative one coulomb.

While the coulomb is the SI unit, you might encounter other units. In the CGS system, there's the 'esu' or electrostatic unit, also called the statcoulomb. One coulomb is equal to 3 times 10 to the power of 9 esu.
For practical applications, especially with batteries, you might see units like the Ampere-hour, which is 3600 coulombs, or the Faraday, used in chemistry, which is about 96,500 coulombs.

sections.title: Methods of Charging
sections.narration: So, how do we actually create a net charge on an object? There are three primary methods we'll discuss: friction, conduction, and induction. The first method is charging by friction, also known as triboelectricity. This happens when you rub two different materials together. For example, when you rub a glass rod with a silk cloth. The rubbing process doesn't create charge; it simply provides the energy to transfer electrons that are already there from one material to the other. In our example, electrons move from the glass rod to the silk cloth. The glass rod, having lost electrons, becomes positively charged, while the silk cloth, having gained those electrons, becomes negatively charged. Different materials have different affinities for electrons. The triboelectric series is a list that ranks materials based on this tendency. When you rub any two materials from the list, the one appearing earlier becomes positive, and the one appearing later becomes negative. The second method is conduction, which is simply charging by contact. If you take a charged object, say a negatively charged metal sphere, and touch it to a neutral metal sphere, some of the excess electrons from the first sphere will flow onto the second one, sharing the charge between them. When you separate them, both spheres are now negatively charged. The third and most interesting method is induction. This allows you to charge an object without even touching it.

sections.title: Charging by Induction
sections.narration: Charging by induction is a clever way to charge a conductor without direct contact with the charging object. Let's walk through the process step-by-step. First, we start with a neutral metallic object, like a sphere, which has an equal number of positive and negative charges distributed uniformly. Now, for step one, we bring a charged object, say a positively charged rod, near the neutral sphere, but we don't let them touch. The positive charge on the rod attracts the free electrons within the neutral sphere. These electrons migrate towards the side of the sphere closer to the rod. This leaves the opposite side of the sphere with a deficiency of electrons, and thus a net positive charge. So, we have induced a separation of charge, but the sphere's total charge is still zero. Step two is to provide a path for charge to flow. We connect the sphere to the earth with a conducting wire. The earth acts as a vast reservoir of electrons. The induced positive charge on the far side of the sphere is very attractive to the electrons in the earth, so electrons flow up from the ground onto the sphere, neutralizing that positive side. The near side remains negatively charged due to the strong attraction of the nearby rod. In step three, while the charged rod is still held in place, we disconnect the grounding wire. This traps the excess electrons we just pulled up from the earth onto the sphere. Finally, in step four, we remove the positively charged rod. Without the rod's attractive force holding the excess electrons on one side, they repel each other and spread out uniformly over the surface of the sphere. The sphere is now left with a net negative charge. Notice that the induced charge is opposite in sign to the inducing charge.

sections.title: Detecting Charge: The Gold-Leaf Electroscope
sections.narration: How can we detect if an object has a static charge? One of the classic instruments for this is the gold-leaf electroscope. It's a simple device, typically consisting of a conducting metal disc or ball on top, connected by a conducting rod to two very thin, fragile leaves of gold foil at the bottom. This whole assembly is insulated from its container, usually a glass flask, to prevent charge from leaking away. Let's see how it works with an uncharged electroscope, where the two gold leaves hang straight down, touching each other. If we bring a charged body, say a negative rod, near the top disc without touching it, we get an induction effect. The negative rod repels the free electrons in the conductor. These electrons are pushed down the rod and accumulate on the two gold leaves. Now both leaves have an excess of electrons, so they are both negatively charged. Since like charges repel, the leaves push each other apart and diverge. If we remove the rod, the electrons redistribute, and the leaves fall back together. Alternatively, if we touch the negative rod to the disc, we charge the electroscope by conduction. Electrons flow from the rod onto the entire conducting post and leaves. Again, both leaves become negatively charged and diverge. In both cases, the leaves diverge, telling us the rod is charged, but this method doesn't tell us if the charge is positive or negative. To determine the sign of the charge, we must start with a charged electroscope. Let's say we've already charged our electroscope so it's positive, and its leaves are already diverged. Now, if we bring a positively charged object near the top, it will repel more positive charges (or attract more electrons upwards) from the leaves, making the leaves even more positive. This increased repulsion causes the leaves to diverge further. If, instead, we bring a negatively charged object near the top, it will attract the positive charges from the leaves up towards the disc. This reduces the positive charge on the leaves, lessening their repulsion, and causing them to converge or fall closer together. So, by observing whether the leaves diverge more or converge, we can determine the nature of an unknown charge.

segments.text: How can we detect if an object has a static charge? One of the classic instruments for this is the gold-leaf electroscope. It's a simple device, typically consisting of a conducting metal disc or ball on top, connected by a conducting rod to two very thin, fragile leaves of gold foil at the bottom.
This whole assembly is insulated from its container, usually a glass flask, to prevent charge from leaking away.

Let's see how it works with an uncharged electroscope, where the two gold leaves hang straight down, touching each other. If we bring a charged body, say a negative rod, near the top disc without touching it, we get an induction effect.

The negative rod repels the free electrons in the conductor. These electrons are pushed down the rod and accumulate on the two gold leaves. Now both leaves have an excess of electrons, so they are both negatively charged.
Since like charges repel, the leaves push each other apart and diverge. If we remove the rod, the electrons redistribute, and the leaves fall back together.

Alternatively, if we touch the negative rod to the disc, we charge the electroscope by conduction. Electrons flow from the rod onto the entire conducting post and leaves. Again, both leaves become negatively charged and diverge.
In both cases, the leaves diverge, telling us the rod is charged, but this method doesn't tell us if the charge is positive or negative.
To determine the sign of the charge, we must start with a charged electroscope. Let's say we've already charged our electroscope so it's positive, and its leaves are already diverged.

Now, if we bring a positively charged object near the top, it will repel more positive charges down to the leaves, making them even more positive. This increased repulsion causes the leaves to diverge further.

If, instead, we bring a negatively charged object near the top, it will attract the positive charges from the leaves up towards the disc. This reduces the positive charge on the leaves, lessening their repulsion, and causing them to converge or fall closer together.
So, by observing whether the leaves diverge more or converge, we can determine the nature of an unknown charge.

sections.title: Example 1: Charge Transfer and Mass
sections.narration: Let's work through an example. A glass rod is rubbed with a silk cloth. The glass rod is found to acquire a charge of positive 19.2 times 10 to the power of minus 19 Coulombs. We need to solve three things. One: find the number of electrons lost by the glass rod. Two: find the negative charge acquired by the silk. And three: determine if there is a transfer of mass from the glass to the silk. For the first part, we use the principle of charge quantization, q equals N times e. The number of electrons, N, is the total charge 'q' divided by the fundamental charge 'e'. We are given that q is 19.2 times 10 to the minus 19 C, and we know e is 1.6 times 10 to the minus 19 C. Plugging in the values, we get 19.2 divided by 1.6, which equals 12. So, the glass rod lost 12 electrons. For the second part, we use the law of conservation of charge. Since the glass rod lost 12 electrons, the silk cloth must have gained those same 12 electrons. Therefore, the charge on the silk is the negative of the charge on the glass rod, which is minus 19.2 times 10 to the minus 19 Coulombs. For the third part, we need to consider if mass was transferred. Since charge is carried by electrons, and electrons have mass, a transfer of electrons means a transfer of mass. The mass of a single electron is about 9 times 10 to the minus 31 kilograms. Since 12 electrons were transferred, the total mass transferred is 12 times the mass of one electron. This calculates to 1.08 times 10 to the minus 29 kilograms. While this mass is non-zero, it is incredibly small and completely negligible in any macroscopic measurement.

sections.title: Coulomb's Law
sections.narration: Now that we understand charge, let's explore the force between charges. This is described by Coulomb's Law, a fundamental principle of electrostatics. The law states that the force between two point charges is directly proportional to the product of the magnitudes of the charges and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them. This 'inverse square' relationship is very important and appears elsewhere in physics, like in Newton's Law of Gravitation. The force is always directed along the straight line connecting the two charges. If the charges have the same sign (both positive or both negative), the force is repulsive, pushing them apart. If they have opposite signs, the force is attractive, pulling them together. Mathematically, we can write this as F equals k times the product of q1 and q2, all divided by r-squared. Here, q1 and q2 are the magnitudes of the two charges, r is the distance between them, and 'k' is the Coulomb constant. In a vacuum, k has a value of approximately 9 times 10 to the power of 9 Newton-meter-squared per Coulomb-squared. This constant 'k' is also written as one over four pi epsilon-naught, where epsilon-naught is another fundamental constant called the permittivity of free space. It represents how easily an electric field can establish itself in a vacuum.

sections.title: Coulomb's Law in a Medium
sections.narration: What happens if the charges are not in a vacuum, but are instead submerged in a material, or medium, like water, oil, or mica? The presence of the material alters the force between the charges. The formula for Coulomb's law is modified to account for this. The force in a medium is given by F equals one over four pi epsilon-naught epsilon-r, times q1 q2 over r-squared. This new term, epsilon-r, is called the relative permittivity or, more commonly, the dielectric constant of the medium, often denoted by the letter K. It's a dimensionless number that tells us how much the medium reduces the electric force compared to a vacuum. Since epsilon-r is always greater than or equal to one, the force between two charges in a medium will always be less than or equal to the force between them in a vacuum at the same distance. We can express the dielectric constant K as the ratio of the force in a vacuum to the force in the medium. For a vacuum or air, K is approximately 1, so the formula simplifies back to the original. For other materials, K is larger. For example, pure water has a very high dielectric constant of about 80. This means the electric force between two charges in water is 80 times weaker than in a vacuum! For mica, it's around 7 to 10. For metals, which are conductors, the dielectric constant is considered to be infinite. This means the electrostatic force inside a conductor is effectively shielded and becomes zero.

segments.text: What happens if the charges are not in a vacuum, but are instead submerged in a material, or medium, like water, oil, or mica? The presence of the material alters the force between the charges.
The formula for Coulomb's law is modified to account for this. The force in a medium is given by F equals one over four pi epsilon-naught epsilon-r, times q1 q2 over r-squared.
This new term, epsilon-r, is called the relative permittivity or, more commonly, the dielectric constant of the medium, often denoted by the letter K.
It's a dimensionless number that tells us how much the medium reduces the electric force compared to a vacuum.
Since epsilon-r is always greater than or equal to one, the force between two charges in a medium will always be less than or equal to the force between them in a vacuum at the same distance.
We can express the dielectric constant K as the ratio of the force in a vacuum to the force in the medium.
For a vacuum or air, K is approximately 1, so the formula simplifies back to the original. For other materials, K is larger. For example, pure water has a very high dielectric constant of about 80.

This means the electric force between two charges in water is 80 times weaker than in a vacuum! For mica, it's around 7 to 10. For metals, which are conductors, the dielectric constant is considered to be infinite.
This means the electrostatic force inside a conductor is effectively shielded and becomes zero.
